Models also struggle to recognize when clarification is necessary. We will release the public split of our benchmark, the model outputs on it, and the evaluation pipeline to support future research.

articles.title: Multi-Objective Causal Bandits: Minimal Intervention Space and Policy-Level Learning
articles.summary: Many decision-making problems involve multiple objectives, where actions affect several performance metrics, fairness criteria, or safety constraints. We study multi-objective causal bandits with…
articles.abstract: Many decision-making problems involve multiple objectives, where actions affect several performance metrics, fairness criteria, or safety constraints. We study multi-objective causal bandits with multiple reward nodes, where actions correspond to interventions on subsets of variables in a causal graph and performance is evaluated through Pareto optimality. Existing approaches to multi-objective bandits often rely on pairwise Pareto dominance or optimize a fixed scalarization. However, pairwise comparisons alone can fail to identify actions dominated by randomized policies, whose expected reward vectors lie in the convex hull of action-level rewards. Thus, an intervention may be suboptimal even if no single intervention dominates it, because it can be dominated by a randomized policy over other interventions. We formalize this policy-level phenomenon and show that it has consequences for both causal action-space reduction and online learning. First, we provide a necessary-and-sufficient graphical characterization of possibly Pareto- optimal minimal intervention sets. Our characterization yields a minimal, sound, and complete candidate intervention family from the graph alone, correcting prior formulations that may include intervention sets that are never Pareto-optimal under any compatible structural causal model. Second, over this reduced intervention space, we design an online UCB-style algorithm that eliminates actions using dominance tests against convex combinations of other actions, and prove logarithmic gap-dependent Pareto regret. Finally, we study constrained multi-objective causal bandits, where feasibility and optimality may be realized only with randomized policies, and develop an online UCB-style constrained bandit algorithm with sublinear regret and constraint-violation guarantees.

articles.title: Robust Well-Log Reconstruction Across Point Gaps and Whole Wells via Boundary-Gated Soft-Thresholding Kalman Fusion
articles.summary: Missing wireline logs hinder subsurface characterization. Deep reconstruction networks suffer from gap-boundary steps and cross-basin shifts, while interpolation and Gaussian smoothers struggle with…
articles.abstract: Missing wireline logs hinder subsurface characterization. Deep reconstruction networks suffer from gap-boundary steps and cross-basin shifts, while interpolation and Gaussian smoothers struggle with long intervals and outliers. We propose boundary-gated soft-thresholding Kalman fusion (ST-KF), unifying multiresolution wavelet shrinkage, distance-gated residual prior learning, and closed-form robust Kalman smoothing with learning--inference decoupling. Across two public benchmarks totaling 263 wells in the Norwegian North Sea and New Zealand's Taranaki Basin, ST-KF ranks first over 0.15--100-m anchored gaps with 0.09% parameter overhead. Against the strongest of nine baselines, pooled RMSE falls by 5.0%--8.3% for bulk density and 6.4%--15.6% for compressional slowness; against the four strongest baselines, reductions are 0.7%--4.1% for neutron porosity and 1.3%--2.9% for photoelectric factor. Ablations and sensitivity analyses confirm operator synergy and stable performance: removing state-space fusion increases short-gap errors by up to 58.8%, while zero-shot transfer cuts anchored errors by 14%--68%. The results show that local borehole continuity transfers across basins whereas cross-property mappings shift with regional geology, supporting measurement-guided log reconstruction.

articles.title: Well-Log Reconstruction with Pre-trained Geological Knowledge: A Knowledge-Conditioned Large-Language-Model Generative Agent
articles.summary: Missing well-log intervals make subsurface reconstruction ill-posed. Existing numerical regression models lack geological prior knowledge to constrain ambiguous inverse mappings.
articles.abstract: Missing well-log intervals make subsurface reconstruction ill-posed. Existing numerical regression models lack geological prior knowledge to constrain ambiguous inverse mappings. We propose GeoLog-Agent, a knowledge-conditioned generative agent using pre-trained large language models (LLMs) as a source of geological priors. A universal Geo-Harness translates LLM stratigraphic reasoning into formation-anchored petrophysical trajectories, feature-wise linear modulation, and conditional adversarial constraints. On the Norwegian North Sea benchmark, GeoLog-Agent achieves a mean $R^2$ of 0.9307 and a peak $R^2$ of 0.9713. It exceeds the nine-baseline average $R^2$ of 0.8387 by 0.0920, with a 30.97% average RMSE reduction, and exceeds the strongest baseline by 0.0274--0.0498 in $R^2$, with 16.25%--24.05% lower RMSE. Ablations confirm the effectiveness and synergy of geological prior reasoning, multi-scale dilated generation, and conditional adversarial modules. Transferring the coupling mechanism to six conventional deep learning models improves their $R^2$ by 0.0162--0.0789 with cross-well stability. These results demonstrate how foundation-model domain reasoning can constrain deep generative reconstruction of missing petrophysical measurements.

articles.title: Before the Word: Name Information in Description-Derived States of Small Language Models, With and Without Naming Failure
articles.summary: The tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state, knowing an object but not its name, motivates this study as an analogy only. We ask whether small language models form a name-predictive state from a name-free…
articles.abstract: The tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state, knowing an object but not its name, motivates this study as an analogy only. We ask whether small language models form a name-predictive state from a name-free description, and whether it differs when naming fails but description selection succeeds. In an internally pre-registered study (a frozen document, no external registry) of Qwen2-0.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B and Phi-3-mini with 200 items, we combine a similarity read-out, a Patchscopes-style read-out and activation patching with matched controls. H1 (name information in the state) was supported in all nine model-by-description-type combinations; the agreement rule was met by the similarity measure together with patching, while Patchscopes stayed near chance. Post-hoc robustness checks after internal review (logit lens, single-position patch, manipulation check) temper this reading: name information in middle layers is clearest under the multi-position patch and the similarity measure, and weak under single-position patching at 50% depth. H2' (description-paraphrase consistency of name-free states not lower in failure items) is mixed: the SmolLM2 deficit test is significant under the pre-registered specification but not robust; Phi-3 non-inferiority holds across margins and a word-overlap covariate, although its bootstrap interval includes zero; Qwen2-0.5B is inconclusive. A capacity explanation remains untested. We report vehicle-level signals only, not meaning.

articles.title: NAP-Wave: A Neural Adaptive Plane-Wave Architecture for High-Frequency Helmholtz Problems
articles.summary: Training neural networks to simulate highly oscillatory wavefields presents optimization challenges, often hindered by spectral bias and poorly conditioned physics-based loss landscapes. To address…
articles.abstract: Training neural networks to simulate highly oscillatory wavefields presents optimization challenges, often hindered by spectral bias and poorly conditioned physics-based loss landscapes. To address these challenges and enhance convergence, we propose NAP-Wave, a joint neural architecture and training strategy that expands the target scattered wavefield in an adaptive neural plane-wave basis. The basis functions are extracted from all hidden layers and modulated by trainable plane-wave carriers, embedding the high-frequency oscillatory physics directly into the network's trial space. NAP-Wave is trained on a physics-informed loss built from the Lippmann-Schwinger integral equation, so no differentiation of the network with respect to its input is required. We develop a decoupled optimization strategy in which Adam updates the parameters of the neural plane-wave basis, while the linear combination coefficients are computed exactly by a least-squares (LS) solver. We couple this with an adaptive-depth training strategy in which the network starts shallow and grows progressively layer-by-layer. At each growth step, we avoid the loss spikes typical of dynamic network growth using the LS-computed coefficients, the warm-started parameters, and the preservation of the first- and second-order optimizer moments of the previous stage. Ablation studies confirm that the plane-wave basis, the exact coefficient solve, and the progressive schedule independently accelerate convergence and improve accuracy. Validated on exact-solution benchmarks, NAP-Wave achieves relative L2 errors of order 1%. On highly heterogeneous geophysical benchmarks, it achieves relative errors of 5%, 9%, and 10%, significantly outperforming published PINN methods in both accuracy and convergence time. To ensure reproducibility, the code is available at https://github.com/Hamza-Kamil/NAP-WAVE.

articles.title: Synthetic Neurosymbolic Task Generation with Controlled Constraint Complexity
articles.summary: We introduce NeSySy, a synthetic generator for neurosymbolic learning tasks that jointly produces logical constraints and consistent datasets. Unlike existing benchmarks, NeSySy provides fine-grained…
articles.abstract: We introduce NeSySy, a synthetic generator for neurosymbolic learning tasks that jointly produces logical constraints and consistent datasets. Unlike existing benchmarks, NeSySy provides fine-grained control over key properties such as constraint structure, tightness, input dependence, and data generation and alignment strategies. In particular, it allows the use of rich constraints over infinite domains, and uses solvers to ensure that the constraints are meaningful and that generated samples satisfy the constraints. We design NeSySy to support both learning with declarative constraints and learning from distant supervision. Across a range of constraint families, we provide evidence that its parameters induce systematic and largely independent effects on task difficulty. Using NeSySy, we study constraint-aware learning methods, identifying regimes where explicit constraint enforcement is beneficial and where expressive unconstrained models can instead learn constraint structure directly from data. Our results establish NeSySy as a controlled testbed for analysing the interaction between learning and logical structure. NeSySy is built around a pipeline that incorporates solvers. Satisfiability checkers (CNFgen and Z3) generate and certify constraints. Constrained optimizers (RC2 for MaxSAT, Z3 for OMT) compute optimal repairs that guarantee every generated sample is consistent.

articles.title: PBit1: One Programmable P-Bit per Parameter - A Finite-Control Representation of Pretrained Networks
articles.summary: We introduce PBit1, a finite-control representation of pretrained neural networks that assigns one programmable p-bit to each learned parameter. A 12-bit command sets its probability, a shared affine…
articles.abstract: We introduce PBit1, a finite-control representation of pretrained neural networks that assigns one programmable p-bit to each learned parameter. A 12-bit command sets its probability, a shared affine range maps that probability to the weight domain, and temporal observations reconstruct the weight for inference. Operator-aware range grouping and sensitivity-based sampling allocation adapt the representation to the network. Across five independent weight draws at 32,768 observations per scalar, selected configurations preserve task quality in GPT-2, DistilBERT, and LFM3-1.7B with every learned scalar converted and no fine-tuning. GPT-2 and LFM3 perplexity increase by approximately 0.66% and 0.26%, respectively, while DistilBERT accuracy changes from 87.51% to 87.49%. A sensitivity-based policy reduces GPT-2 reconstruction observations by 41.7% while retaining the quality criterion. Complete-model evaluations reuse reconstructed weights in BF16 inference, and THRML operator experiments examine native sampling and spatial-temporal tradeoffs. Together, these results establish PBit1 as a concrete construction for studying finite-control weight representation and temporal reconstruction in pretrained networks.

articles.title: Explicit Regularization for Flow Matching
articles.summary: Learning the underlying probability distribution from samples is a core problem in statistics and applied mathematics. Generative models based on diffusion and flow matching learn a velocity field…
articles.abstract: Learning the underlying probability distribution from samples is a core problem in statistics and applied mathematics. Generative models based on diffusion and flow matching learn a velocity field whose flow transports a known distribution to the data distribution. They produce novel, realistic samples, although the empirical learning problem is ill posed near the data distribution. Its minimizer transports the samples onto the training data, and small perturbations of the data change the velocity field strongly near the end of the flow. The observed generalization is often attributed to implicit regularization by the network parameterization, early stopping of the training, and the time integration during sampling. Explicit regularization has advanced the theory and computation of many inverse problems and has recently been proposed to prevent memorization in generative models. With a regularizer on the magnitude of the velocity, however, the field approaches the memorizing velocity unless the regularization parameter grows to infinity fast enough, and it then stays bounded by a constant that is small only for large parameters. We show that penalizing the derivatives of order $k$ of the velocity renders the $D$-dimensional empirical problem well posed uniformly in time if $2k > D$ and the training points are in general position. Our experiments in one and two dimensions discretize the velocity with splines and use direct solvers for the regularized least-squares problems to exclude optimization error. Refining the discretization in space and time changes the error of the Hessian-regularized flows only marginally, whereas without the regularizer the error tends to that of memorization. These flows generalize, with errors comparable to or lower than those of well-tuned kernel density estimates.

articles.title: SLiDE: Structured Linear Dynamics for Forecasting with Exogenous Inputs
articles.summary: Accurate time series forecasting with exogenous inputs is critical across domains, including energy and retail, yet modern deep learning models often overfit to correlations that do not generalize…
articles.abstract: Accurate time series forecasting with exogenous inputs is critical across domains, including energy and retail, yet modern deep learning models often overfit to correlations that do not generalize under shifts in these inputs. We propose SLiDE, a Koopman-inspired architecture for forecasting with exogenous inputs that imposes structure on latent temporal dynamics. SLiDE approximates nonlinear system evolution using a learned linear operator in a latent space, combining (i) a history encoder that reconstructs the current latent state from past targets and inputs with (ii) a shared linear rollout driven by future exogenous variables. By enforcing a common linear recurrence across encoding and prediction, SLiDE aligns how past information is encoded with how future states evolve, reducing parameterization and preventing reliance on spurious correlations in the input history. Empirically, SLiDE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on real-world benchmarks, including electricity price forecasting and retail demand, while maintaining a computational footprint comparable to lightweight MLP architectures. SLiDE is especially effective at generalizing to shifted exogenous inputs, reducing MSE by 20% on electricity price samples with out-of-range exogenous values and MAE by 30% in a synthetic transfer setting where the same dynamical system is driven by an unseen exogenous process. Ablations confirm the importance of both the structured history encoder and the linear latent rollout, suggesting that structured latent linear dynamics provide a useful inductive bias for forecasting with exogenous inputs.

articles.title: Risk-Averse Decision-Focused Learning: Minimizing CVaR of Regret
articles.summary: Many combinatorial optimization (CO) problems involve parameters that are uncertain when the problem must be solved. In such settings, the parameters have to be predicted from correlated contextual…
articles.abstract: Many combinatorial optimization (CO) problems involve parameters that are uncertain when the problem must be solved. In such settings, the parameters have to be predicted from correlated contextual information before a solution can be computed. \emph{Decision-focused learning} (DFL) addresses this by training the predictive model to produce predictions that optimize downstream decision quality. Most existing DFL methods are risk-neutral and minimize the expected regret. In high-stakes applications this can lead to undesirable outcomes, because decision-makers must also account for the tail risk of decision quality. Prior risk-sensitive approaches typically model uncertainty explicitly and solve a stochastic or robust optimization problem at inference time, which increases computational complexity. We instead propose a DFL framework that achieves risk-sensitive behavior while retaining point predictions and deterministic optimization at inference time. Starting from the dual representation of the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) and adding entropy regularization, we derive a smooth surrogate for the CVaR of regret. Its gradient induces an instance-dependent reweighting within each minibatch that emphasizes high-risk outcomes, so the approach can turn existing surrogate-loss DFL methods, including the SPO+ loss, into risk-sensitive variants. When instantiated with SPO+, the resulting objective admits a generalization bound on the CVaR of the true regret. Experiments on knapsack, portfolio, shortest-path, and energy-aware scheduling problems show substantial reductions in tail regret when the uncertain parameters exhibit heterogeneous tail behavior.

articles.title: Spectral Steering: Local Inverse Geometry for Frozen Diffusion Generators
articles.summary: A frozen diffusion generator may need to change several output properties while preserving others. We study when guidance faithfully realizes such a structured request and whether local inverse…
articles.abstract: A frozen diffusion generator may need to change several output properties while preserving others. We study when guidance faithfully realizes such a structured request and whether local inverse correction improves its direction. Our account links this benefit to the interaction between the request and the objective-specific remaining-sampler Jacobian: conditioning alone is insufficient. Spectral steering combines a request-specific cosine-gain predictor with damped inverse correction and fixed-time relinearization for finite edits. Scalar nulls and matched-movement controls test the predicted mechanism. Across 8,923 instances in a retrospectively identified local regime, predicted and realized gains correlate at Spearman 0.79, versus -0.11 for condition number. Experiments span images, audio, robotics, and control and planning, including complex character motion generation. On 50 paired inpainting cases, four corrections improve unobserved-pixel PSNR over Adam by 3.25 dB at equal total derivative traversals. Together, the analysis and controls connect request-dependent geometry to directional gains and establish where these gains translate into downstream performance.

articles.title: Bellman Residual Bracketing: Resolving the Sample Complexity of Discounted and Average-Reward RL
articles.summary: We study the sample complexity of the empirical planning or plug-in approach for reinforcement learning (RL) with a generative model. We show the discounted plug-in approach finds an…
articles.abstract: We study the sample complexity of the empirical planning or plug-in approach for reinforcement learning (RL) with a generative model. We show the discounted plug-in approach finds an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy with $O(SA (1-γ)^{-3} \varepsilon^{-2} \log(SA/δ))$ samples, where $S, A, γ, δ$ are the state and action sizes, discount factor, and failure probability, respectively. In the average-reward setting, we show that discounted plug-in and direct (undiscounted) plug-in achieve $O(SAH\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/δ))$ and $O(SAD\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/δ))$ complexities, respectively, where $H$ upper-bounds the optimal bias span and $D$ is the diameter. Combining with our lower bounds for nonadaptive generative models, these results resolve the minimax sample complexity of discounted RL and average-reward RL --- in both the span- and diameter-based classes --- up to constant factors. Our main technical contribution is a novel Bellman residual bracketing technique which improves the efficiency of prior absorbing-MDP-based concentration analyses.

articles.title: Sharp First-Hit Identification from Finite Depth Samples
articles.summary: Which depths in a new camera view are determined by finitely many source-depth measurements? Pointwise uncertainty bounds do not answer this question: unobserved geometry between samples can change…
articles.abstract: Which depths in a new camera view are determined by finitely many source-depth measurements? Pointwise uncertainty bounds do not answer this question: unobserved geometry between samples can change which surface is encountered first. We study a bounded Lipschitz class of continuous source inverse-depth fields with interval observations and known camera pose. Building on classical Lipschitz envelopes, we characterize the exact set of attainable first-hit depths and construct a globally admissible scene for every value in that set. The set can be disconnected. We also give a necessary and sufficient test for several proposed depths to be first hits of one shared scene. An epipolar reduction uses scalar cone inequalities without enumerating surfaces. In a rectified model with source spacing $h$, interval half-width $\varepsilon$, baseline $b$, and slope bound $L$, we prove a sharp worst-case inverse-depth diameter of $\max\{Lh+2\varepsilon,2\varepsilon/(1-bL)\}$ when $bL<1$, subject to sufficient depth and domain range for attainment. Exact samples still give the sharp bound $Lh$ at $bL=1$, while above this threshold ambiguity need not vanish as sampling becomes arbitrarily dense. Any positive measurement uncertainty can destroy uniform stability at the critical threshold. We provide constructive examples, an exact rational validation oracle, and a frozen ten-scene evaluation using reference, stereo, and learned-depth observations. The experiments separate solver correctness under the scene assumptions from failure of those assumptions: fixed learned-depth bands often yield narrow but incorrect sets. The results identify what a specified scene class permits; they do not infer a continuum regularity or physical-scene guarantee from sampled predictions.

articles.title: Read, Then Shade? How Visual Evidence Changes Incentive-Driven Misreporting in Vision-Language Advisors
articles.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly read a scene and report it to someone who acts on the report, sometimes under objectives that differ from that person's. We ask whether a stated incentive…
articles.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly read a scene and report it to someone who acts on the report, sometimes under objectives that differ from that person's. We ask whether a stated incentive moves what a VLM reports, and whether this changes when the value must be read from pixels rather than given as text. In seeded synthetic scenes, a model reads the position of a target on a labelled axis and reports one integer to a fixed receiver; it is paid, in simulation, for accuracy or for a report a few units to one side, and every scene is also presented with the true value as text. Across a pilot and three follow-up studies with hash-frozen protocols, four small open VLMs from three families, and 15,170 held-out trials, a stated payoff moved reports in both modalities, and exact compliance at three units was significantly lower with the image than with text for three of four models; Qwen2.5-VL 7B showed no reliable difference. Adding the true value as text to the image prompt removed the gap in every model. For InternVL3 the gap vanished on scenes it read correctly when it wrote its reading first; for Gemma 3 it persisted. For Qwen2.5-VL 3B, which read every scene correctly, the gap held in four of five payoff paraphrases, nearly vanished when the model wrote its reading before its report or when the prompt stated that the client wants the truth, vanished with an unpaid goal, and persisted when the model reported before stating its reading; how often it shaded at all, even with text, depended strongly on the wording. When told that the client wants the true value, three of four models still shaded every text report. Visual input did not make these advisors reliably more truthful; it made compliance with a stated incentive depend on whether the read value is made explicit and on output order, a dependence that text-only evaluations and mean-shift metrics do not reveal.

articles.title: Steering Bayesian Inference and Decisions through Data Poisoning
articles.summary: Adversarial machine learning has revealed that statistical models can be manipulated through poisoned data, and Bayesian inference is no exception. Earlier work has shown that subtle poisoning…
articles.abstract: Adversarial machine learning has revealed that statistical models can be manipulated through poisoned data, and Bayesian inference is no exception. Earlier work has shown that subtle poisoning attacks can drive the posterior toward a distribution of the attacker's choosing. Such posterior attraction attacks require a fully specified target posterior; however, attackers typically care about only a few posterior quantities or, more consequentially, about a downstream decision. Herein, we study how an attacker can alter Bayesian inference and decisions by deleting or replicating a few observations, chosen to minimize the maximum mean discrepancy between the resulting posterior and a target distribution. A suitable kernel lets the attacker steer selected posterior moments without specifying the rest of the target. Because Bayes actions depend on the posterior only through expected utilities, which are themselves posterior moments, the same approach can target a decision directly. We construct the attacks with a gradient-based heuristic that requires only posterior samples, and analyze its convergence. Experiments with regression and hierarchical models compare moment-based and full-posterior attacks, and illustrate how deleting a handful of observations can flip a Bayesian decision.

articles.title: Random Cut Forests, Games and Diffusion over Approximately Nested Anisotropic Local Geometry
articles.summary: Just as the data in a dynamic stream changes, questions asked of the stream also change in intent: what to hold constant, which counterfactuals to consider, and so forth. Energy-based learning has…
articles.abstract: Just as the data in a dynamic stream changes, questions asked of the stream also change in intent: what to hold constant, which counterfactuals to consider, and so forth. Energy-based learning has been celebrated for its uniform approach to losses and estimation, but interpretability remains challenging. Tree-based methods, on the other hand, offer high interpretability but often rely on bespoke, disjointed estimators. Neither paradigm readily supports changing questions on streaming data. In this paper we take a step towards combining energy, interpretability, and streaming. Random cut forests retain an evolving geometry of the data. We study this geometry as the basis for diffusion dynamics, prediction, explanation, and games. We show that several existing scores are escape probabilities of random walks on the trees. The induced affinity is realized exactly by a sparse electrical network on each tree, giving a single energy calculus, a Hamiltonian, maintained along one path per update. This connects an estimate, its supporting evidence, and the response to intervention through the same boxes, gaps, masses, and paths. Different questions correspond to different clamp decisions on the energy. Fixing observed values gives harmonic prediction with Gaussian uncertainty. Fixing a partition gives normalized cuts whose cost is attributed exactly to oriented faces. Releasing clamps gives coalition games, in which collusive displacement measures the field response. With noise, the same energy gives diffusion dynamics whose relaxation rates are read from the boxes. Axis-parallel cuts localize at a rate set by affine rather than ambient dimension, and this control passes to the averaged energy. Across a forest the boxes are only approximately nested; common reference observations align the trees. A rotating star with added noise illustrates the measurements.

articles.title: Func-JEPA: Learning a Sobolev Space of Functions as Latent Vectors
articles.summary: Pretraining an encoder once and reusing it across tasks is a widespread approach in vision and language. However, neural symbolic mathematics still trains a dedicated sequence-to-sequence model for…
articles.abstract: Pretraining an encoder once and reusing it across tasks is a widespread approach in vision and language. However, neural symbolic mathematics still trains a dedicated sequence-to-sequence model for each task, so that no representation of a function is shared. In this work, we propose the Function Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Func-JEPA, abbreviated f-JEPA): an encoder of mathematical functions, pretrained on their symbolic form, whose latent space imitates the Sobolev space H^1 and in which differentiation is a learned latent operator. The norm of a latent is computed exactly from the function, whereas its direction is learned to match Sobolev angles. The frozen encoder is then reused by lightweight modules for decoding, composition, integration, and regression from samples. The representation and four downstream tasks are evaluated within and outside the pretraining distribution. f-JEPA recovers exact formulas from noisy samples more often than the compared symbolic-regression methods, whereas computer algebra and task-specific models remain stronger on standard integration and differential-equation benchmarks.

articles.title: Geometric Stability and Sample Complexity for Compositional Function Priors
articles.summary: We study when compositional structure yields dimension reduction in supervised learning. We frame learning as empirical risk minimization with a function-space prior: a regularization functional…
articles.abstract: We study when compositional structure yields dimension reduction in supervised learning. We frame learning as empirical risk minimization with a function-space prior: a regularization functional selects a subset of functions with favorable approximation and metric entropy. The models are compositions $f(x)=g(Ax+Δh(x))$, where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$ is a linear base map, $Δh$ is a nonlinear correction, and $g$ is an outer function; that is, $f$ is an arbitrary smooth function of a $k$-dimensional representation of the input that is linear up to a correction. We prove covering-number bounds showing that the statistical complexity of this class interpolates between an intrinsic regime, parametric in the $kd$ entries of the linear map and nonparametric only in the representation dimension $k$, and an ambient $d$-dimensional nonparametric rate; the interpolation is controlled by the correction size $\varepsilon=\|Δh\|$. We then connect $\varepsilon$ to data geometry. If the data lie in a small tube around a $k$-dimensional manifold and the regression target depends on the input only through its nearest point on that manifold, then locally the target factorizes exactly as $g(Ax+Δh(x))$ with $A$ a tangent chart and a correction whose Sobolev norm scales linearly with curvature at the localization scale. Patching such local models over an atlas gives a finite-sample excess-risk bound for a least-squares estimator over a finite net of local models, whose ambient term vanishes with curvature. For a one-dimensional model problem we also prove a converse: on curved data, every affine compositional predictor faces an error floor unless its correction budget scales with curvature, while the matching curved model class attains the intrinsic rate. The correction size $\varepsilon$ is thus the effective-dimension parameter linking curvature to statistical complexity.

articles.title: Equilibrium measures for anisotropic exponential interaction energies with applications to transformers
articles.summary: We study the minimization of anisotropic exponential interaction energies over probability measures on the sphere, motivated by mean-field models of self-attention in transformer architectures. For…
articles.abstract: We study the minimization of anisotropic exponential interaction energies over probability measures on the sphere, motivated by mean-field models of self-attention in transformer architectures. For every symmetric positive definite interaction matrix, we relate the minimizer to a corresponding anisotropic Brownian motion and use the Feynman--Kac formula and elliptic regularity theory to show that it admits a smooth, strictly positive density on the sphere. We further show that it is the only stationary measure with full support for the dynamics considered. We use the stochastic viewpoint to derive an algorithm for sampling from the minimizer. In dimension two, we also propose a numerical scheme for approximating its density based on a Mathieu series expansion.

articles.title: Over-the-Air Semantic Alignment via Dual Stacked Intelligent Metasurfaces
articles.summary: Semantic communications enable task-oriented information exchange, but suffer from latent-space mismatch when transmitter and receiver employ heterogeneous machine learning models. Existing semantic…
articles.abstract: Semantic communications enable task-oriented information exchange, but suffer from latent-space mismatch when transmitter and receiver employ heterogeneous machine learning models. Existing semantic alignment methods rely on digital processing, introducing computational and latency overhead. This paper proposes a dual stacked intelligent metasurfaces (dual-SIM) architecture that performs semantic alignment entirely in the wave domain. By jointly exploiting programmable metasurfaces at both ends of a link and the wireless channel, the proposed architecture realizes an end-to-end linear transformation between heterogeneous latent spaces. We show phase-only multilayer SIM can approximate both supervised linear aligners and zero-shot Parseval-frame equalizers. We investigate single-SIM, disjoint asymmetric and symmetric dual-SIM, and jointly optimized dual-SIM configurations, considering channel equalization and constructive channel exploitation. For joint design, we develop an alternating projected gradient algorithm with convergence guarantees to first-order stationary points. We further introduce a deep-unrolled network that unrolls gradient-based iterations to reduce computational cost of SIM reconfiguration under channel variations. Numerical results with heterogeneous vision transformer encoders show accurate semantic alignment from moderate to high signal-to-noise ratios. The joint and symmetric disjoint dual-SIM designs achieve the highest accuracy over compact channels, the joint design leads at shallow stack depths, and the advantage over single-SIM designs diminishes at equal depth.

articles.title: Evaluating and Improving Natural Language Autoencoders
articles.summary: Natural language autoencoders (NLAs) are a method for generating natural language explanations of LLM activations. We develop evaluations based on auditing tasks that test the ability of NLAs to…
articles.abstract: Natural language autoencoders (NLAs) are a method for generating natural language explanations of LLM activations. We develop evaluations based on auditing tasks that test the ability of NLAs to surface latent knowledge, identify whether a model was misled by a hint, and catch a silent fabrication. We also develop extensions to NLAs that let them use activation information from multiple layers and positions, let us apply them more effectively to long transcripts, and reduce the number of false claims they make. These extensions result in improvements on both our auditing evaluations and auxiliary evaluations adapted from prior work. We also use the evaluations to study how different auditing capabilities change over the course of NLA training, and find that although every evaluation improves early in training, extended training can hurt performance on some of our auditing evaluations.

articles.title: Do Probing and Steering Favor the Same Directions Within and Across Language Models?
articles.summary: A direction in a language model's hidden state can be used to probe whether a concept is present or to steer the model toward it. Although probe directions are often reused for steering, the…
articles.abstract: A direction in a language model's hidden state can be used to probe whether a concept is present or to steer the model toward it. Although probe directions are often reused for steering, the direction that best detects a concept need not be the one that best changes it. We study this distinction in three instruction-tuned models from different families. We construct a one-parameter family of directions ranging from a covariance-adjusted discriminant to the mean difference, and evaluate probing and additive steering, which adds the direction to the hidden state, along the family at a fixed side effect. For truthfulness and sentiment, in every model, the best probe is not the best steering direction: steering consistently favors directions closer to the mean difference. This separation holds across 59 of 60 layer-model-concept combinations in a layer sweep, with matched probe and steering texts in all six model-concept combinations, and under a rotation-based steering operator. The exact steering optimum is less stable: for sentiment, an intermediate direction produces a 27-56% stronger steering effect than the mean difference, but this gain shrinks or disappears with matched texts and depends on the layer and the operator. The two roles also transfer differently across models. A probe transferred by a linear map fitted on neutral text retains 81-91% of the target model's above-chance probing performance, while the transferred mean difference retains less of its steering effect in 11 of 12 model pairs. This is a consistent tendency, although our predefined criteria classify only three pairs, and nine remain inconclusive. Finally, as an application on PopQA, steering toward "unknown" increases abstention by 18-44 percentage points on uncertain errors, versus 2-5 on confident errors, while rarely correcting errors in cases where a correct answer is reachable.

articles.title: Probing SAM Perturbations Through Statistical Replay
articles.summary: Sharpness Aware Minimization (SAM) updates model parameters using gradients evaluated at adversarially perturbed weights, but it remains unclear which aspects of this procedure are sufficient to…
articles.abstract: Sharpness Aware Minimization (SAM) updates model parameters using gradients evaluated at adversarially perturbed weights, but it remains unclear which aspects of this procedure are sufficient to reproduce its generalization behavior. In our ResNet 18 experiments on CIFAR 10, simple curvature regularizers based on the Hessian trace and largest eigenvalue remain below SAM in validation accuracy, motivating a direct examination of its perturbations. We introduce statistical replay, a diagnostic that summarizes perturbations from reference SAM trajectories using elementwise means and standard deviations over local windows and constructs new perturbations during independent SGD training. Pure replay uses only these summaries, whereas mixed replay adds isotropic Gaussian noise. Pure replay does not reproduce SAM's validation behavior, while mixed replay and pure isotropic perturbations can approach its validation performance at selected scales without reproducing its training dynamics. An equal radius random direction within SAM performs similarly to SGD, and source, temporal, and layer interventions further suggest that replay behavior depends on perturbation construction. Together, these preliminary results weaken several simple explanations of SAM while leaving an important part of its mechanism unexplained.

articles.title: Grokking Can Be Steered: Selecting Desirable Solutions By Choice Of Learning Rule
articles.summary: During grokking, a network transitions from memorization to generalization, yet what shapes the neural implementation (circuit) of the generalizing solution and specifically the number of…
articles.abstract: During grokking, a network transitions from memorization to generalization, yet what shapes the neural implementation (circuit) of the generalizing solution and specifically the number of participating neurons (its size) remains unclear. We find that the learning rule, the combination of credit assignment algorithm and optimizer, controls this: On modular addition, every learning rule we study that groks recovers the same Fourier-based algorithm, yet implemented by circuits that differ in size. Why? A neuron stays in use when its credit is large relative to the non-gradient term of its own update, and this single condition unifies three routes to unused neurons: the coupled weight decay, Adam's $ε$ and the decay of a trainable per-neuron gain. Equalizing the magnitude of credit assigned to each neuron, or scaling each neuron's weight decay by its credit, expands the effective circuit size, measured from the outgoing weights, from 60% to 99% of the layer's neurons at similar training and test accuracy. We vary which neurons share one equalization factor, from the whole layer to individual neurons, and find that the circuit stays concentrated for groups of eight or more and fully distributes only when every neuron has its own factor. Credit magnitudes are usually set by the normalization of standard optimizers: Nero, which normalizes per neuron, distributes the computation, whereas Adam and seven others, including RMSProp, Muon, and Shampoo, use other normalization schemes and retain small, concentrated circuits. Distributed circuits tolerate neuron deletion better, while concentrated circuits can be pruned further and transfer about twice as fast to a task that recombines the same features, largely by recruiting their unused neurons. Learning rule choice thus steers circuit size, trading robustness against compressibility and transfer speed without changing the learned algorithm.

articles.title: Interpreting Random Forests: Comparing Surrogate Models and Rule Extraction Methods
articles.summary: Random forests (RFs) often achieve high prediction performance, but their ensemble structure can be difficult to interpret. Surrogate models and rule extraction methods offer interpretable…
articles.abstract: Random forests (RFs) often achieve high prediction performance, but their ensemble structure can be difficult to interpret. Surrogate models and rule extraction methods offer interpretable approximations, yet guidance on selecting an appropriate method for a specific research question remains limited. We compared 12 methods for interpreting RFs, with a decision tree as a prediction-oriented reference, across 11 simulation settings and 67 benchmark datasets for regression and classification. Evaluation addressed prediction and structural similarity to the RF, model complexity, prediction performance, and runtime. Simulations additionally assessed explainability using known effect and noise variables. No method performed best across all objectives. For regression, SLIM provided the strongest general performance for prediction similarity or performance on test data, while a linear model offered a simpler global interpretation of linear effects when performance was comparable. For classification, inTrees achieved the strongest overall benchmark performance, with CTree and OC-CART providing useful alternatives. ART consistently produced the most compact representations. NH and SIRUS offered strong structural similarity for regression, while MRT most closely reproduced RF variable usage in the classification simulations, illustrating that prediction-oriented rankings do not necessarily identify the best structural explanation. Outcome-type restrictions, runtime limits, and method-specific failures reduced result availability for several approaches and should be considered alongside performance when selecting a method. Method selection should therefore be guided by the outcome type, anticipated data structure, and intended interpretability objective. Prediction similarity alone is insufficient for explaining an RF and should be considered jointly with structural similarity and model complexity.

articles.title: Successive Convexification in Learned World Models for Safe Offline Planning
articles.summary: World models learned from offline data allow an agent to plan without further interaction with the environment, but the sampling-based planners used with them handle safety constraints only by…
articles.abstract: World models learned from offline data allow an agent to plan without further interaction with the environment, but the sampling-based planners used with them handle safety constraints only by scoring or rejecting sampled action sequences. We instead pose safe planning in the latent space of a learned world model as a successive convex program (SCP), in which a learned discrete-time control barrier function is imposed as a constraint at every step of the horizon. SCP requires smooth dynamics, so we build the networks from smoothed MaxMin activations and spectrally normalised layers, and bound the resulting linearisation error in terms of the Lipschitz bound and the smoothing width. As SCP is a local method, we start it from a sampled plan. On two Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks with offline data, this planner has fewer violations than MPPI and CEM drawing 128 times as many samples at equal wall-clock time in our main comparison, though not significantly, and earns greater return at longer horizons, and is much safer than SCP without a sampled start. SCP converged more often on Lipschitz-bounded models. Unlike sampling, it also reports at each step whether its plan is a feasible, first-order optimal KKT point of the planning problem in the model, or that no feasible plan was found nearby. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/youngers2006/scwm.

articles.title: Predicting, Fast and Slow: SSD Already Knows Which Guess Is Wrong
articles.summary: Heimdall, a learned controller, calls slow on 52% of an SSD's reads when 30% are slow. Uncertainty estimators, the remedy prescribed for its wrong guesses, cannot find them: nine of them do no better…
articles.abstract: Heimdall, a learned controller, calls slow on 52% of an SSD's reads when 30% are slow. Uncertainty estimators, the remedy prescribed for its wrong guesses, cannot find them: nine of them do no better than a coin. The drive can. On one trace, 2% of the reads of 4 to 8 KiB that found less than 4 KiB outstanding while the drive was answering came back slow, and Heimdall called 96% of them slow. A 4,096-entry table of how the drive's recent reads came back, untrained and 21 ns a decision, ranks the wrong guesses at a median AUROC of 0.68 on 57 held-out traces, where the nine sit at 0.46 to 0.52, and it predicts slow reads better than Heimdall itself.

articles.title: Efficient and Accurate Causal Validation of Training Data Attribution
articles.summary: Causal validation of training data attribution (TDA) methods is costly, since evaluation involves retraining a model on many different subsets of the original training set. For example, the Linear…
articles.abstract: Causal validation of training data attribution (TDA) methods is costly, since evaluation involves retraining a model on many different subsets of the original training set. For example, the Linear Datamodeling Score (LDS), which has become a standard metric for evaluating TDA methods, measures the correlation between TDA predictions and expected retrained model outputs. In this paper, we reduce the amount of computation needed to estimate the LDS along three axes: the number of sampled training subsets, the number of retraining seeds per subset, and the number of models in the attribution ensemble. Each of these factors induces a form of bias in the LDS estimation, and removing these sources of bias significantly reduces the number of retrainings needed to match the same accuracy in LDS estimation. On ResNet-9/CIFAR-10, finite-subset debiasing achieves $3.2\%$ relative RMSE with as few as $4$ subsets, and $32$ subsets match the accuracy of ordinary Spearman using $96$ subsets, measured against a 300-subset reference. On ResNet-9/CIFAR-10, BERT/QNLI and GPT-2/WikiText-2, estimating the training-noise variance allows us to reproduce the standard five-seed LDS at the same accuracy with $2$--$5\times$ fewer retrainings.

articles.title: Architectures and KV Replay for Depth-Recurrent Language Models
articles.summary: Depth recurrence increases effective model depth by repeatedly applying a fixed computation block. However, sharing attention parameters does not share the key-value (KV) states generated at…
articles.abstract: Depth recurrence increases effective model depth by repeatedly applying a fixed computation block. However, sharing attention parameters does not share the key-value (KV) states generated at different recurrence iterations, which causes memory growth with recurrence depth during autoregressive decoding. We study how to reduce this memory cost through architectural and cache-sharing approaches within a common depth-recurrent framework. We first study a looped hybrid that repeats a stack of Transformer layers, with recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks replacing most attention layers and periodic Transformer attention anchors retained. We then restrict recurrence to a dedicated recurrent workspace in a Parcae-style architecture and test its stabilising adapter as a wrapper for the looped hybrid. Finally, we train a looped Transformer with recurrent KV replay, where only selected recurrence iterations write KV states that later iterations reuse. This trains the model to operate with the same shared KV topology used during inference. We find that looped hybrids require sufficiently frequent attention anchors, with performance depending strongly on the recurrent mixer. For cross-iteration KV sharing, recurrent KV replay allows multiple recurrence iterations to reuse the same KV states while retaining performance close to the full looped Transformer with separate KV caches for each iteration.

articles.title: Federated versus Centralized PV Capacity-Factor Forecasting: A Non-Inferiority Study Across Seven Stations in North Macedonia
articles.summary: Background: Photovoltaic (PV) forecasts inform energy commitments by PV operators and aggregators and guide charge-discharge scheduling in solar-plus-storage systems. Federated learning enables…
articles.abstract: Background: Photovoltaic (PV) forecasts inform energy commitments by PV operators and aggregators and guide charge-discharge scheduling in solar-plus-storage systems. Federated learning enables collaborative model training through model updates when local operators cannot pool raw operational data. This study evaluated whether federated training was non-inferior to centralized training for PV capacity-factor prediction across seven stations in North Macedonia. A common multilayer perceptron was used in an offline forecasting comparison with a 24-hour timestamp lag. Exploratory validation compared local, centralized, Federated Averaging, and Federated Proximal (FedProx) training. FedProx (E = 1, mu = 1) was selected for a confirmatory comparison under a protocol fixed before test evaluation. The comparison used past-only offline inputs, five paired training seeds, macro-averaged mean absolute error (MAE), a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.005, and a paired day bootstrap with 10,000 repetitions over 49 test dates. Results: FedProx achieved a macro-MAE of 0.128397, compared with 0.133405 for centralized training. The paired difference (FedProx minus centralized) was -0.005008 (95% confidence interval: [-0.009926, -0.000537]). The upper confidence bound was below the prespecified margin, satisfying the non-inferiority criterion. All five seed-specific differences favored FedProx, and its mean MAE was lower at six of the seven stations. Post hoc calendar sensitivity analyses did not change the conclusion. Conclusions: These findings support further evaluation of federated forecasting for collaboration under data-pooling constraints. The study demonstrates predictive non-inferiority within the evaluated setting. Benefits for energy commitments and battery scheduling remain potential applications requiring operational evaluation.

articles.title: Do Pretraining Optimizer Gains Transfer to KL Distillation?
articles.summary: Matrix-structured optimizers can improve language-model pretraining, but it is unclear whether these gains transfer to short-horizon KL distillation from an instruction-tuned initialization. We…
articles.abstract: Matrix-structured optimizers can improve language-model pretraining, but it is unclear whether these gains transfer to short-horizon KL distillation from an instruction-tuned initialization. We compare AdamW and diagonal AdaGrad with two tractable Shampoo reductions, SOAP, and All-2D Muon across four dense Qwen student-teacher pairs under a common forward-KL objective and fixed training budget. Across scales, none of the evaluated matrix-structured recipes consistently improves the quality versus trainer-time trade-off over the elementwise references: AdamW generally attains the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be slightly faster at larger scale. SOAP often tracks AdamW in KL but incurs substantial trainer-time overhead, and the two Shampoo reductions reverse ordering across model pairs, showing that conclusions depend on the feasible recipe. These results suggest that pretraining optimizer gains do not transfer automatically to KL distillation and should be re-established for the target objective and systems regime.

articles.title: PMR: MoE Routing with Shared Prototypes and Congestion Pricing
articles.summary: Conventional linear routers in sparse mixture-of-experts models select experts directly from token-expert matching scores, coupling input matching with expert allocation. We propose…
articles.abstract: Conventional linear routers in sparse mixture-of-experts models select experts directly from token-expert matching scores, coupling input matching with expert allocation. We propose Prototype-Mediated Routing (PMR), a two-stage router with shared prototypes. PMR first computes each token's distribution over prototypes, then uses it to mix prototype-conditioned expert distributions according to the law of total probability. This formulation models input matching and expert allocation separately, explicitly represents many-to-many associations between prototypes and experts, and provides separate interfaces for context adaptation and load regulation. Within this framework, short-term states summarize preceding tokens to adapt the prototypes, while congestion prices updated from dispatch feedback achieve loss-free load balancing by adjusting the conditional expert distributions. We use a two-pass blockwise approximation to accelerate short-term state processing, achieving over 20 times the training throughput of the eager tokenwise PMR implementation while maintaining high agreement in routing decisions. Across three pretraining configurations with 0.43B, 1.18B, and 0.48B total parameters, PMR improves mean zero-shot accuracy on seven benchmarks over linear routing baselines with matched expert architectures by 1.54, 2.65, and 1.45 percentage points (pp), respectively. The corresponding gains on ARC-Easy are 6.71, 5.80, and 3.92 pp. In parameter-efficient fine-tuning of 7B-8B backbones, PMR's improvements over MixLoRA vary across backbones, with gains of up to 1.76 pp in mean accuracy across four tasks.

articles.title: Confidence Without Cause: Predicting and Localizing Physics-Shortcut Sensitivity in Language Model Hidden States
articles.summary: A language model's confidence on a physics problem deserves trust only if it ignores details irrelevant to the answer. We introduce DECOY (Distractor-Embedded Certified cOunterfactuals for phYsics):…
articles.abstract: A language model's confidence on a physics problem deserves trust only if it ignores details irrelevant to the answer. We introduce DECOY (Distractor-Embedded Certified cOunterfactuals for phYsics): 155 families of four prompts differing in one irrelevant detail. A symbolic solver certifies that each edit preserves the answer. Families are labelled by the largest drop in the model's log-probability of the certified answer, using a threshold fixed before probe training. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is sensitive on 50.0% of the 140 families yielding labels, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 22.9%. Effects are largest when distractor values lie numerically close to the answer. A linear probe on Qwen's layer-18 hidden state, averaged over four renderings, predicts sensitivity before generation at AUROC 0.760 with whole families held out. A separately tuned single-rendering probe reaches 0.747. A frozen layer-16 probe reaches 0.820 pooled AUROC on 15 families built after training, though within-cue-type AUROC is lower (0.667-0.6875). Under a paired family bootstrap, the probe performs on par with a fitted token-entropy baseline (AUROC 0.727) and achieves the lowest Brier score among tested predictors (0.204 versus 0.214). Knocking out four attention heads at layer 16 cancels sensitivity on a 20-family panel, localising it to a narrow mechanism. These results show that Qwen's confidence can track irrelevant details, that this failure is detectable before generation, and that targeted intervention can suppress it. DECOY provides certified ground truth and paired-tested baselines for evaluating hidden-state monitors.

articles.title: Generalization Bounds for Neural Networks with Sparse Connectivity
articles.summary: Empirical evidence suggests that large neural networks rarely make effective use of all available parameters, with learned solutions exhibiting pronounced sparsity. Despite this ubiquity, existing…
articles.abstract: Empirical evidence suggests that large neural networks rarely make effective use of all available parameters, with learned solutions exhibiting pronounced sparsity. Despite this ubiquity, existing generalization theory only partially explains how such sparsity influences statistical performance. In this paper, we derive non-asymptotic generalization gap bounds for deep neural networks whose layer-wise weight matrices are restricted by $\ell_p$ quasi-norm ($0<p\leq 1$) constraints. Our analysis gives rise to a novel result that interpolates between classical norm-based generalization guarantees and parameter-counting bounds. Remarkably, in the extreme sparsity limit as the quasi-norm order $p$ approaches zero, our analysis reveals a transition to a square-root dependence on the number of \emph{active} (non-zero) parameters, resulting in bounds that are strictly tighter than existing parameter-counting approaches. Experiments demonstrate that our bounds exhibit a milder dependence on initial architectural choice at the over-parametrization regime, effectively capturing the generalization benefit of the sparsity arising from training on natural data.

articles.title: Test-Time Constraint-Aware Diffusion Predictive Control
articles.summary: Diffusion models can learn multimodal distributions over finite-horizon state-input sequences, providing a way to generate candidates for predictive control. However, sequences generated by a…
articles.abstract: Diffusion models can learn multimodal distributions over finite-horizon state-input sequences, providing a way to generate candidates for predictive control. However, sequences generated by a pretrained model may violate safety constraints introduced at deployment, for example when obstacles are added or repositioned. Retraining whenever these constraints change limits the usefulness of learned predictive controllers. In this paper, we propose Test-Time Constraint-Aware Diffusion Predictive Control (TCA-DPC), an algorithm for adapting the sampling distribution of a pretrained diffusion controller to newly introduced safety constraints without retraining. We treat the pretrained model as a prior over finite-horizon sequences and define an adapted distribution through exponential tilting based on a constraint-violation penalty. The tilt strength is adjusted online using the fraction of generated sequences that fail constraint verification. We approximately sample the adapted distribution using the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm in the Gaussian noise space of the pretrained diffusion sampler.

articles.title: $β$-number and Its Applications to Data Science
articles.summary: In this paper, we introduce a novel metric, $β$-number, designed to measure the "$p$-th order $d$-dimensional oscillation degree" of a set. For a given set $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$,…
articles.abstract: In this paper, we introduce a novel metric, $β$-number, designed to measure the "$p$-th order $d$-dimensional oscillation degree" of a set. For a given set $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$, $β$-number is computed by identifying an optimal $d$-dimensional plane $L$ that minimizes the average $p$-th order distance of all points in $K$ to $L$. This metric serves as a versatile tool in data science, functioning both as a dimensionality reduction technique to find the optimal $p$-th order $d$-dimensional subspace and as a measure to characterize data oscillation for classification. We conduct a thorough exploration of $β$-number through theoretical analysis and numerical experiments. Initially, we establish the upper and lower bounds of $β$-number for any set $K$, along with its scaling law. We then elucidate the relationships between $β$-number and its related parameters. A key finding of this study is that in discrete settings, when $p=2$, the $d$-dimensional plane determined by $β$-number coincides with that obtained via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), positioning $β$-number as a generalization of PCA. Furthermore, we propose two algorithms for calculating $β$-number in both continuous and discrete settings. We validate our theoretical results through a series of numerical experiments in low-dimensional cases. Finally, we demonstrate the potential of $β$-number in practical data analysis through a dimensionality reduction task and an image classification task.

articles.title: Enforcing Ellipsoidal Constraints in Neural Networks with a Polynomial Safety Layer
articles.summary: Often the output of a learned mapping must satisfy prescribed constraints. In the control of autonomous systems, for example, the chosen action must keep the system within a collision-free region.
articles.abstract: Often the output of a learned mapping must satisfy prescribed constraints. In the control of autonomous systems, for example, the chosen action must keep the system within a collision-free region. We consider the case in which a proposed output is corrected by projection onto a safety ellipsoid. Computing this projection amounts to solving a quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP). We construct a neural-network safety layer by unrolling a feasibility-preserving polynomial penalty iteration. The unrolled structure allows the loss gradient to propagate from the feasible output through the safety layer to the network parameters during training. We show how to choose the layer parameters so that every iterate is feasible and give a computable bound on its distance to the exact projection at any prescribed depth. We illustrate the method by training a LiDAR-based policy to control an unmanned aerial vehicle. A privileged model predictive control expert uses the map and the measured vehicle state to generate the training data. In the simulated narrow mazes, the filtered policy avoided wall contact at every tested stage of training, including at initialization, when every unfiltered flight hit a wall. A representative build of the learned policy and its safety layer for an Arm Cortex-M4F microcontroller occupies about 36 KiB of flash, with a RAM budget below 5 KiB.

articles.title: A Comparative Evaluation of BERT-Based and LLM-Based Models for Indic Sentence Similarity
articles.summary: The relative effectiveness of BERT-based encoders and large language model (LLM)-based embeddings for Indic semantic textual similarity remains insufficiently characterized. We compare eight…
articles.abstract: The relative effectiveness of BERT-based encoders and large language model (LLM)-based embeddings for Indic semantic textual similarity remains insufficiently characterized. We compare eight BERT-based and five LLM-based models on the 1,500-pair STS Benchmark development set translated into ten Indic languages and on the native Marathi MahaSTS test set. IndicSBERT achieves the highest Pearson correlation in all ten translated language sets, with a macro-average of 0.843, followed by BGE-M3 at 0.792. Harrier-270M is the strongest LLM-based model on translated STS-B, with a macro-average of 0.751. On MahaSTS, IndicSBERT and Bhasha-Embed-v0 achieve Pearson correlations of 0.901 and 0.900, respectively, while EmbeddingGemma leads the LLM-based models at 0.871. The highest-scoring BERT-based model thus exceeds the highest-scoring LLM-based model in both settings, although the magnitude of the difference varies across benchmarks. These findings indicate that LLM-derived embeddings do not uniformly improve Indic sentence similarity over established encoders and motivate evaluation that accounts for language coverage, task supervision, and benchmark construction.

articles.title: SMELL: Sparsity-aware Memory Efficient Federated Fine-tuning for Long-context LLMs
articles.summary: Federated fine-tuning enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to collaboratively adapt to distributed private data. However, long-context fine-tuning on resource-constrained devices faces substantial…
articles.abstract: Federated fine-tuning enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to collaboratively adapt to distributed private data. However, long-context fine-tuning on resource-constrained devices faces substantial challenges arising from excessive activation memory, heterogeneous token-importance patterns across clients, and communication overhead. To address these challenges, we propose SMELL, a Sparsity-aware and Memory-Efficient federated fine-tuning framework for Long-context LLMs. SMELL integrates three complementary mechanisms: Local Sparse-Forward Adaptation (LSFA), Consensus-Anchored Sparsity Coordination (CASC), and Communication-Efficient Progressive Update Recovery (CPUR). These mechanisms jointly enable memory-efficient local adaptation, heterogeneity-aware sparsity coordination, and lightweight model-update transmission. Experiments on OPT-350M and LLaMA2-7B demonstrate that SMELL reduces peak memory consumption by up to 88.35% compared with conventional fine-tuning and 13.25% compared with forward-only LoRA fine-tuning at a 16K context length. Furthermore, SMELL improves fine-tuning performance under certain non-IID settings and supports compact update transmission with progressive reconstruction, demonstrating its potential for resource-efficient federated long-context LLM adaptation.

articles.title: Attention U-Net Cellular Automata for Multi-Class Land Use and Land Cover Change Simulation in Lucknow, India: Evaluation Against Null and Classical Baselines
articles.summary: Convolutional networks are often used to learn the transition rules of land-use cellular automata (CA), yet their predictions are seldom compared with a null model that predicts no change. We built…
articles.abstract: Convolutional networks are often used to learn the transition rules of land-use cellular automata (CA), yet their predictions are seldom compared with a null model that predicts no change. We built AttentionUNet-CA, which reads a 32 x 32 neighbourhood of land-cover states with four drivers (elevation, distance to major roads, distance to the central business district (CBD) and population density) and predicts the state of each cell ten years later. We tested it on Lucknow, India, with GLC_FCS30D land cover for 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2020, a 30 m series mapped consistently over time, and compared its built-up class with GHSL and ESA WorldCover. AttentionUNet-CA was trained on 1990-2010, selected on held-out spatial blocks and evaluated once on 2010-2020, with three seeds. Baselines were the null model, a random-forest CA (RF-CA) and a U-Net CA without attention; each network was trained with and without class weights. Only 8.1% of the study area changed in the test decade, so no model matched the overall agreement of the null model (91.9%). On change, measured by the figure of merit, the class-weighted networks scored highest (U-Net CA 22.0 +/- 1.2%, AttentionUNet-CA 21.0 +/- 1.4%), ahead of RF-CA (20.3%), but by margins comparable to seed-to-seed variation; the networks estimated the amount of change better than RF-CA. The attention gates did not improve accuracy. Population density and distance to the CBD were the most useful drivers. Projected to 2030, built-up land grows by 22-35%, mostly at the city edge.

articles.title: Information Limits of Replay-Free Recurrent State Migration
articles.summary: When a recurrent model is replaced, its old state may not determine what the new model would compute from the same history. We characterize the information that must be retained before the…
articles.abstract: When a recurrent model is replaced, its old state may not determine what the new model would compute from the same history. We characterize the information that must be retained before the replacement is known. For a time-invariant affine linear family, the minimum continuous causal memory for order-$k$ local migration equals the reachable dimension of a lifted coefficient system minus the information in the anchor state. A controllable $d$-state model with scalar input needs at most $kd$ additional real coordinates, even when arbitrary matrix replacement directions are revealed only after streaming. A single rank-one direction can already require all $kd$. Conditional singular values and auxiliary-bit bounds distinguish this local information law from recovery at a fixed tolerance. We also give invariant-subspace and future-output constructions. Controlled experiments compare the resulting representations. In a small language model, equal-memory cubic interpolation improves mean state fidelity over third-order coefficients but provides no meaningful predictive gain. An analytic history basis preserves useful adaptation more economically in a coupled identification task. With repeated slow poles, eight history coordinates meet normalized output error $10^{-4}$ across five fitted seeds despite substantial full-state error. Splitting the poles raises the smallest tested successful width to 64.

articles.title: Delay-Aware Reinforcement Learning for O-RAN Control under Stochastic Reward Feedback
articles.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly employed for real-time control in Open Radio Access Networks (O-RANs). However, the asynchronous nature of O-RAN feedback introduces stochastic delays…
articles.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly employed for real-time control in Open Radio Access Networks (O-RANs). However, the asynchronous nature of O-RAN feedback introduces stochastic delays between actions and their observable rewards, leading to misaligned credit assignment and unstable training. This letter formulates the O-RAN control problem as a Markov decision process (MDP) with delayed and stochastic rewards, where the true reward corresponding to an action is received after an unknown delay. To address this, we propose a delay-aware deep RL framework that integrates a long short-term memory (LSTM)-based delay predictor and a temporal reward realignment module within an off-policy learning pipeline. Using empirical delay traces collected from the Open AI Cellular (OAIC) testbed, we demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves faster convergence and significantly reduces latency violations and packet drops compared to conventional RL methods that ignore feedback delay. The results confirm that reward-delay compensation is critical for reliable AI-driven O-RAN control.

articles.title: From Mutation to Medication: Characterizing Failures of Clinical LLMs to Respect Genomic Resistance
articles.summary: Language models are increasingly proposed to support molecular tumour boards, but may recommend cancer therapies despite genomic evidence of resistance. We evaluated ten models on 1,464 resistance…
articles.abstract: Language models are increasingly proposed to support molecular tumour boards, but may recommend cancer therapies despite genomic evidence of resistance. We evaluated ten models on 1,464 resistance cases from five curated oncology knowledge bases, collecting 58,910 judgments. Models endorsed resisted therapies in 21.8-81.4% of cases. However, raw rates can reflect a tendency to agree rather than an ability to distinguish resistance from drug sensitivity: one open-weight model endorsed 81.4% of resistance cases and 82.3% of sensitivity controls. We therefore compared endorsement within matched gene and evidence-level groups. This analysis is exploratory because it was specified after the pre-registered analysis, which yielded null-to-weak results. Measured failures depended strongly on the reference knowledge base and evidence strength. When a second source independently confirmed resistance, four models across three vendors endorsed at most 2.4% of cases; at weaker evidence tiers, discrimination was not measurable. Models sometimes acknowledged resistance yet recommended the therapy. Repeating a model's own resistance conclusion reduced endorsement to 0.0-3.5% on cases where it had stated resistance. Falsely attributing the opposite conclusion increased endorsement above baseline for all seven hosted models, reaching 95.2% for GPT-4o; an instruction without an attributed conclusion changed endorsement by only 0.9 percentage points. Providing the correct curated evidence reduced unqualified strong recommendations to 0.3-3.5%, testing evidence use under an oracle condition rather than retrieval.

articles.title: Benchmarking the State of AI for Crop Yield Forecasting: A Global Assessment Across Modeling Paradigms
articles.summary: Accurate crop yield forecasting is essential for food security, agricultural policy, and commodity markets. Although statistical, process-based, and machine learning approaches have all been…
articles.abstract: Accurate crop yield forecasting is essential for food security, agricultural policy, and commodity markets. Although statistical, process-based, and machine learning approaches have all been proposed, their relative strengths remain poorly understood due to the lack of large-scale, standardized comparisons. We address this gap through a comprehensive benchmark of five modeling paradigms -- statistical baselines, process-based models, conventional feature-engineered machine learning, deep sequence models, and tabular foundation models -- using the CY-Bench benchmark spanning 63 country-crop datasets (>12,000 administrative regions) across six continents. Beyond conventional pooled accuracy metrics, we introduce a multi-dimensional evaluation framework that separately quantifies overall, spatial, temporal, and anomaly prediction skill. Across multiple crops and countries, feature-engineered machine learning and tabular foundation models achieve the strongest overall predictive performance. Data-driven models reduce NRMSE in 72% of countries growing maize and 78% of countries growing wheat, with median reductions of 8.8% and 11.9%, respectively. Across all modeling paradigms, spatial prediction is substantially easier than temporal and anomaly prediction. While data-driven models markedly improve temporal and anomaly prediction over statistical baselines, accurately forecasting year-to-year yield variability remains challenging. These findings suggest that future progress in large-scale crop yield forecasting will depend on the improved characterization of the environmental and management factors driving inter-annual yield variability, founded on effective representations for crop yield forecasting systems that support agricultural decision-making, early-warning applications, and food security planning

articles.title: Gradient-Based Co-Design of Systems and Reinforcement Learning Policies with Differentiable Simulators
articles.summary: Co-design is the problem of jointly optimizing the design of a system and the policy that operates it. Neither can be chosen independently: a system design is only as good as the policy trained for…
articles.abstract: Co-design is the problem of jointly optimizing the design of a system and the policy that operates it. Neither can be chosen independently: a system design is only as good as the policy trained for it, and the optimal policy changes with the design. When that policy is learned by reinforcement learning (RL), evaluating a candidate design requires a full policy training run, and the design is usually optimized by black-box search such as Bayesian optimization (BO) or evolution strategies (ES). These methods scale poorly with the design dimension and ignore the differentiable structure of modern simulators and, in particular, the sensitivity of the optimal policy with respect to the design.
